reference_title: Design and Construction of Continuous Flight Auger Piles

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations of CFA Piles
sections.summary: CFA piles are favorable in medium to very stiff clays, cemented sands, residual soils, medium-dense to dense silty sands, and rock overlain by stiff soil. Unfavorable conditions include very soft soils (risk of necking), loose sands below groundwater (high mining risk), geologic voids or flowing water, hard strata overlain by soft or loose soil (flighting), and profiles requiring piles longer than 30 m. Applications requiring significant shear, bending, or uplift resistance are generally not suitable for CFA piles due to limitations on reinforcement placement depth.
sections.body:
CFA piles generally work well in medium to very stiff clay soils, cemented sands or weak limestone (stable during drilling, good bond), residual soils (especially silty/clayey with small cohesion), medium-dense to dense silty sands and well-graded sands, and rock overlain by stiff or cemented deposits (pile bears on rock with competent overlying soil).

Installation is problematic in: very soft soils (difficulty controlling volume per unit length, risk of necking or bulging from oversupply); loose sands or very clean uniformly graded sands under groundwater (high soil mining potential — DD piles more reliable in these conditions); geologic formations with voids, pockets of water, lenses of very soft soil, or flowing water; hard soil or rock overlain by soft or loose granular soil (slow penetration through hard stratum causes flighting of overlying loose soils); sand-bearing stratum underlying stiff clay (slow rate in clay causes flighting of sand from bearing stratum, resulting in near-zero end-bearing); highly variable ground conditions; very hard strata requiring CFA auger penetration; piles longer than 30 m (100 ft) requiring unusual equipment; and conditions with deep scour or liquefiable sand where high bending resistance is required.

Project conditions favoring CFA piles: projects where installation speed is important (production rates of 300–450 m/day for private work, 60–150 m/day for transportation); batter piles limited to 1:4 or steeper; large numbers of piles; low headroom conditions (more cost-effective than micropiles if ground conditions are favorable); secant or tangent pile walls up to about 10 m (33 ft) exposed height; soundwall foundations; and pile-supported embankments.
key_points: Favorable soils: medium to very stiff clay, cemented sands, residual soils, medium-dense to dense sands, rock under stiff overburden
Unfavorable: very soft soils (necking), loose water-bearing sands (mining), voids/flowing water, hard stratum under soft soil
Sand-bearing stratum under stiff clay: slow drilling in clay causes flighting of sand; pile carries only side friction
Piles >30 m (100 ft) require unusual high-torque equipment; deep-scour/liquefiable zones require high bending resistance
Project favoring conditions: speed-critical, large quantities, low headroom, secant walls ≤10 m, soundwalls, pile-supported embankments
Applications requiring significant uplift, shear, or bending are generally not suitable due to rebar placement limitations

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations of Drilled Displacement Piles
sections.summary: Drilled displacement (DD) piles install by laterally displacing soil rather than extracting it, resulting in no or minimal spoil, densification of loose sands around the pile, increased horizontal stress, and higher unit side resistance in granular soils compared to conventional CFA piles. DD piles are less susceptible to soil flighting in mixed profiles with loose granular interbeds. Limitations: much greater torque required than CFA piles limits maximum depths to about 20–25 m (65–80 ft) and precludes use in dense/hard soils. Cannot be used in rock.
sections.body: Drilled displacement (DD) piles have many of the same features, advantages, and limitations as CFA piles. Key differences: (1) Better performance in loose sandy soils — DD piles increase horizontal stress and densify the ground during installation, achieving ground improvement and higher side-shear resistance in granular soils. DD piles are generally less subject to soil flighting problems, and in general will achieve a given load carrying capacity at a shorter length than a CFA pile of similar diameter. (2) Little or no spoil removed from site — advantageous where contaminated ground exists or spoil disposal is restricted. (3) Difficult to penetrate dense or hard soils and more limited depth range — because of much greater torque requirements, penetrating deeply into soils with strong resistance may be impossible or impractical; DD piles are generally not installed deeper than about 20 to 25 m (65 to 80 ft). DD piles are not used in rock or even weak rock or hard cemented soils (where CFA piles may be used). (4) Effect of displacement — in confined areas or near utilities/sensitive structures, lateral displacement of soil can affect nearby structures. Closely spaced DD piles can also cause large pore pressures in loose fine-grained soils.
key_points: DD piles densify surrounding soil, increase horizontal stress — higher side resistance in granular soils vs. CFA
Little or no spoil generated — favorable for contaminated sites or restricted disposal areas
Max depth ~20–25 m (65–80 ft) due to high torque demand; cannot be used in rock or hard soils
Lateral displacement can affect nearby utilities and structures; large pore pressures possible in loose fine-grained soils

sections.title: Applications for Transportation Projects
sections.summary: CFA piles are applied in four main transportation contexts: (1) soundwall foundations — single piles at each column, 450–900 mm (18–36 in.) diameter, 4–8 m (13–26 ft) deep, lateral load governed by wind overturning; (2) bridge piers and abutments — best for interchange structures where scour is not a major issue; (3) retaining structures — secant or tangent pile walls up to about 10–18 m (33–60 ft) depth, diameters limited to about 1 m (40 in.), full-length reinforcing cage or structural steel insert; (4) pile-supported embankments — economical for soft soil sites, cycle times ≤15 min/pile, costs ~$40/LM for small diameters.
sections.body:
Soundwall foundations: CFA pile foundations for soundwalls are a straightforward application. Soundwall foundations typically have single piles at each column location with reinforcement or anchor bolts for a moment connection to the column. Typical diameter: 450 to 900 mm (18 to 36 in.) and depth: 4 to 8 m (13 to 26 ft). Foundation design is controlled by overturning from wind loads. CFA piles are an alternative to drilled shafts for soundwall foundations.

Bridge piers and abutments: CFA pile foundations are feasible for bridges in favorable conditions. Most suited are interchange structures where scour is not a major issue, approach structures, and bridge widening projects. CFA piles may be favored where pile driving vibrations or noise requirements cannot be met. The Krenek Road Bridge in Texas (Vipulanandan et al. 2004) is an example: 64 CFA piles, 450 mm (18 in.) diameter, 17–19 m (56–62 ft) long in stiff clay with sand layers. The piles achieved higher-than-anticipated side friction but near-zero end-bearing in the dense sand bearing stratum (decompression during clay drilling). Lesson: CFA piles in this profile should have been designed to terminate in clay.

Retaining structures: CFA piles can form secant or tangent pile walls similar to drilled shaft walls. Diameters generally limited to about 1 m (40 in.). Maximum depths generally 10–18 m (33–60 ft). Control of verticality is critical for watertight structures. For secant walls, primary piles use weaker concrete and secondary piles use stronger mix for structural strength. Reinforcing cage or structural steel section may be used.

Pile-supported embankments: CFA piles offer installation speed and economy for embankment support on soft or compressible soils. Cycle times of 15 minutes or less per pile are achievable. Costs on the order of $40 per linear meter ($12/LF) are feasible for large-volume projects using 300–350 mm (12–14 in.) diameter piles. Design must address edge stability, pile cap design, and reinforced embankment fill overlying piles.
key_points: Soundwalls: single piles 450–900 mm dia., 4–8 m deep, wind-governed lateral load design
Bridge foundations: best for interchanges without scour concerns; CFA can match driven pile economics
Krenek Road case: zero end-bearing in dense sand due to clay drilling decompression — CFA should have terminated in clay
Retaining walls: secant/tangent, diameters ≤1 m, depths ≤18 m; verticality control critical for watertight walls
Pile-supported embankments: ≤15 min/pile cycle time; ~$40/LM for 300–350 mm piles on large projects

sections.title: Construction Cost Evaluation
sections.summary: CFA pile costs on private projects typically range from $40–$60/LM ($12–$20/LF) for 300–450 mm (12–18 in.) diameter piles, with higher costs on transportation projects due to fewer piles per move, performance/integrity testing requirements, and site constraints. U.S. transportation project examples: Texas SH 7 (760 mm piles): $200/LM ($60/LF) plus $25k mobilization and $25k per load test; Kansas DOT (400–450 mm): $72–$85/LM ($22–$26/LF); Florida DOT soundwalls (760–900 mm): $200–$260/LM ($60–$80/LF).
sections.body:
Because the use of CFA piles in U.S. transportation facilities has been very limited, there are few records of cost data for transportation projects. Costs of CFA piles on private projects often range from approximately $40 to $60 per linear meter ($12 to $20 per linear foot) for 300- to 450-mm (12- to 18-in.) diameter piles. However, these projects typically include much greater quantities of piling and fewer moves across the site than is typical for a bridge or soundwall project; prices on transportation projects are likely to be higher. Costs relating to performance and integrity testing are likely to be higher on transportation projects. Many variables affect pile costs, including length, diameter, reinforcement, and grout strength. Costs also vary by region.

Examples from U.S. transportation projects: Texas State Highway 7, Houston County: 760 mm (30-in.) diameter piles; $200/LM ($60/LF), with $25,000 mobilization and $25,000 per static load test. Kansas DOT (bridges and secant pile wall, 400–450 mm): $72–$85/LM ($22–$26/LF); low headroom work at $320/LM ($98/LF). Florida DOT soundwalls (760–900 mm, depths <9 m): $200–$260/LM ($60–$80/LF); 6–15 piles per day production.
key_points: Private projects: $40–$60/LM ($12–$20/LF) for 300–450 mm dia.; transportation projects cost more
Transportation premium: fewer piles per rig move, higher testing costs, site constraints
Texas SH 7 (760 mm): $200/LM + $25k mobilization + $25k per load test (2005 bid price)
Kansas DOT (400–450 mm): $72–$85/LM; Florida DOT soundwalls (760–900 mm): $200–$260/LM
